medical.title: ADHD medication amplifies brain response to grammatically ambiguous sentences, study finds
medical.summary: In a neuroimaging study published in PNAS, a team of researchers led by the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen recorded the brain activity of healthy adults during sentence comprehension after raising catecholamine levels with stimulant medication (methylphenidate). Higher catecholamine levels led to stronger recruitment of cognitive resources during processing of grammatically ambiguous sentences, showing how neurochemical systems may shape language processing.

medical.title: Neural network spots previously missed epilepsy signs on brain MRIs
medical.summary: Researchers from the joint Biomedically-Informed AI Laboratory of Skoltech (a VEB.RF Group institution) and the University of Sharjah and their colleagues have improved the performance of computer vision algorithms that look for signs of epilepsy and multiple sclerosis on brain MRI scans. Rather than merely analyzing an image as a set of pixels, the neural network now also attends to medical features known to physicians. This is complemented by the machine's capability to spot subtle details that elude the human eye. In the future, such solutions will help doctors diagnose diseases and select treatment strategies.

medical.title: National study finds decline in drug use–associated heart infections but growing share involves stimulants
medical.summary: A new national study found that hospitalizations for serious heart infections associated with drug use are declining after years of increases, driven largely by a decrease in opioid-associated cases.

medical.title: 3D-printed implant prototype combines brain activity recording with targeted cooling
medical.summary: Researchers affiliated with the Leibniz Institute of Polymer Research Dresden (IPF) and the Else Kröner Fresenius Center (EKFZ) for Digital Health at TU Dresden have developed a 3D-printed implant prototype that combines the recording of brain activity with targeted cooling. The technology could pave the way for alternative approaches to treating drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The research is published in the journal Advanced Science.

medical.title: Guideline on shorter-course radiation therapy for localized prostate cancer updated
medical.summary: An updated clinical guideline from the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of hypofractionated radiation therapy for patients with localized prostate cancer. The guideline replaces ASTRO's 2018 recommendations and reflects a matured evidence base showing that shorter-course radiation therapy can maintain cancer control while reducing overall treatment burden for patients receiving definitive external beam radiation therapy (EBRT). The guideline was published in Practical Radiation Oncology.

medical.title: How our blood vessels age from within
medical.summary: With every heartbeat, blood is pumped through a vast network of vessels throughout our body, delivering vital oxygen, nutrients and other essential substances to even its most remote corners. But these vessels are far more than passive tubes: Their inner walls are covered by a thin layer of specialized cells called endothelial cells, which regulate blood flow, control what passes into surrounding tissues and help coordinate responses to injury.

medical.title: More than half of children under 5 exposed to hep B exposed via household contact
medical.summary: More than half of children younger than 5 years exposed to hepatitis B virus (HBV) are exposed by someone in their household other than their birth mother, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

medical.title: Rising rates of colorectal cancer found in nearly all age groups
medical.summary: Colorectal cancer rates are rising across younger and older age groups, according to a study published in NEJM Evidence.

medical.title: A doctor's take on new menopause guidelines
medical.summary: Many women I see in my practice have questions about menopause and hormone therapy. The newest guidelines from the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists (ACOG) bring some welcome clarity.

medical.title: IDSA: Cabotegravir + rilpivirine long-acting antiretroviral therapy beneficial in HIV
medical.summary: Cabotegravir + rilpivirine (CAB+RPV) long-acting (LA) antiretroviral therapy (ART) consistently maintains virologic suppression among virologically suppressed adults with HIV, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

medical.title: Deep brain stimulation improves new neuron maturation for memory
medical.summary: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has traditionally been used to treat movement disorders and more recently some mental health disorders such as certain forms of depression, but research has suggested it can affect learning and memory as well.

medical.title: Initial treatment for lower back pain is associated with subsequent risk of opioid use disorder and overdose
medical.summary: Adults on Medicaid who began treatment for a new bout of low back pain with a higher-dose opioid prescription were about two and a half times as likely to later show signs of opioid use disorder or overdose, according to a study conducted at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

medical.title: IDSA: Earlier introduction of HPV vaccine improves initiation, completion by age 13
medical.summary: Introducing the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine at ages 9 to 10 years rather than 11 to 12 years leads to a meaningful difference in initiation and completion of the vaccine series, including initiation and completion by age 13 years, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

medical.title: How blocking immune cell signals could make brain tumors easier to remove
medical.summary: In a new study published in Cancer Cell, researchers at VIB-KU Leuven reduced the spread of glioblastoma by interrupting specific interactions between the brain's immune cells and tumor cells. The discovery points to a possible new therapeutic strategy, in which blocking communication between immune and cancer cells makes tumors more contained and easier to remove.

medical.title: Do more cannabis stores near schools mean more teens use cannabis? Our research suggests the answer is complicated
medical.summary: When Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, one concern was that more legal stores would make cannabis easier for young people to access and encourage adolescent use. But does having more cannabis retailers near high schools actually mean more students use cannabis?

medical.title: Pathology research identifies potential new target for preventing brain metastasis
medical.summary: Research led by professor of pathology Mikhail Nikiforov, Ph.D., has identified a key mechanism that helps cancer cells spread to the brain, which may lead to a new target for future therapies. The findings were published in the journal Cell Reports in the article "SERINC2-mediated phosphatidylserine remodeling activates protrusion-localized AXL signaling to promote brain metastasis."

medical.title: Medicare's prior-authorization pilot test led to an immediate drop in use of services
medical.summary: For many years, traditional Medicare has operated almost entirely without prior authorization, a requirement that clinicians obtain approval before certain services will be covered. The practice is controversial because it adds paperwork, outside review and other barriers that can delay or deny coverage for recommended treatment. While prior authorization is widely used by commercial insurers and Medicare Advantage, traditional Medicare has historically almost never required it.

medical.title: Viruses obey the laws of physics—understanding why they infect people differently could lead to better treatments
medical.summary: The beauty of physics at the cellular scale is part of what draws biomedical engineers and biologists like us to the field of mechanobiology: the study of how physical forces influence biology.

medical.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
medical.summary: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.

medical.title: Blood pressure pregnancy clue could open door to new treatments
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust have uncovered a hidden defect in the tiny blood vessels of women with preeclampsia, a dangerous and common pregnancy complication that can threaten the lives of both mother and baby.

medical.title: Higher medical fees increase expected pain and reduce willingness to book appointments
medical.summary: Rising out-of-pocket medical costs do more than drain a patient's bank account. New research from Carnegie Mellon University shows that high health care prices cause people to expect greater physical pain during medical procedures, driving many patients to skip necessary appointments altogether.

medical.title: Most childhood physical abuse perpetrated within the home, new study finds
medical.summary: New Curtin University–led research has revealed most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families—and before children turn 10.

medical.title: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease.

medical.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.

science.title: New election forecast updates predictions every 10 minutes
science.summary: From Alaska to Texas, the battle for control of the U.S. Senate is unfolding across 35 races. And a new Northwestern University election model is tracking them all—every 10 minutes.

science.title: Halloween meets history in many ghostly tourism attractions. Is this a problem?
science.summary: Halloween, the fall holiday and $13.5 billion industry, lurks around the corner.

science.title: Brambles are a problem weed in South Africa, but researchers are closer to finding a natural enemy to manage them
science.summary: Invasive alien brambles have been spreading across South Africa since the early 1900s, having come from North America and Europe. All brambles fall within the genus Rubus. Their common names in South Africa are braam (Afrikaans), ijingijolo (isiZulu) and monoko-metsi (seSotho).

science.title: 40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
science.summary: Forty years after the Chornobyl disaster, tiny radioactive particles still linger in the soil, carrying a dangerous legacy. Using powerful X-rays, scientists discovered that some of these particles have remained surprisingly stable, trapping radioactive substances inside instead of releasing them into the environment.

science.title: Nearly 3,000 exploding stars challenge our understanding of the Universe
science.summary: A massive analysis of 2,884 exploding stars has uncovered new evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the universe’s expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a cornerstone of modern cosmology and could reshape our understanding of how the universe works.

environment.title: Persian leopards hang on in the Caucasus despite landmines
environment.summary: There have been few sightings of the endangered Persian leopard in the Caucasus region over the past 20 years: just three in Georgia and 10 in Armenia. But scientists and conservationists are alert to one Persian leopard in particular, whom they’ve named Aren and who is presumed to have journeyed 240 kilometers (150 miles) through […]

environment.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.

environment.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
environment.summary: Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. The breakthrough could provide new insights into cancer, infectious diseases, and how drugs interact with cells.

environment.title: NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
environment.summary: Australia's normally dry, rust-colored outback has erupted into a spectacular carpet of wildflowers after unusually heavy rains, potentially producing its most impressive bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellite images capture the stunning transformation, which has even brought rare flowers to the grounds of a remote deep-space observatory.

environment.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
environment.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.

environment.title: NASA spots a giant patch of Moon-like rock on Earth
environment.summary: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed a remarkable formation in Madagascar that looks surprisingly similar to the Moon’s bright highlands. Made of anorthosite, a rock abundant on the lunar surface, the formation dates back at least 600 million years and bears the scars of ancient continental collisions.

environment.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
environment.summary: Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.

environment.title: Earth’s center is moving, and NASA just measured it
environment.summary: Earth’s center of mass is constantly on the move, shifting by a few millimeters as enormous amounts of water, ice, and even air migrate around the planet with the seasons. NASA scientists have developed a more precise way to track these tiny swings using laser-ranging satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.

mix_items.title: The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks
mix_items.summary: A national monument since the 1920s, Chiricahua is America’s newest national park.

mix_items.title: MapInsights helps police trainees learn the territory
mix_items.summary: In early 2026, the University of Illinois Division of Public Safety was facing a challenge. It had 11 security guards it planned to convert to community service officers, which meant they would change from being based in one building to working a whole beat.

mix_items.title: New election forecast updates predictions every 10 minutes
mix_items.summary: From Alaska to Texas, the battle for control of the U.S. Senate is unfolding across 35 races. And a new Northwestern University election model is tracking them all—every 10 minutes.

mix_items.title: Halloween meets history in many ghostly tourism attractions. Is this a problem?
mix_items.summary: Halloween, the fall holiday and $13.5 billion industry, lurks around the corner.

mix_items.title: Brambles are a problem weed in South Africa, but researchers are closer to finding a natural enemy to manage them
mix_items.summary: Invasive alien brambles have been spreading across South Africa since the early 1900s, having come from North America and Europe. All brambles fall within the genus Rubus. Their common names in South Africa are braam (Afrikaans), ijingijolo (isiZulu) and monoko-metsi (seSotho).

mix_items.title: ADHD medication amplifies brain response to grammatically ambiguous sentences, study finds
mix_items.summary: In a neuroimaging study published in PNAS, a team of researchers led by the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen recorded the brain activity of healthy adults during sentence comprehension after raising catecholamine levels with stimulant medication (methylphenidate). Higher catecholamine levels led to stronger recruitment of cognitive resources during processing of grammatically ambiguous sentences, showing how neurochemical systems may shape language processing.

mix_items.title: Neural network spots previously missed epilepsy signs on brain MRIs
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the joint Biomedically-Informed AI Laboratory of Skoltech (a VEB.RF Group institution) and the University of Sharjah and their colleagues have improved the performance of computer vision algorithms that look for signs of epilepsy and multiple sclerosis on brain MRI scans. Rather than merely analyzing an image as a set of pixels, the neural network now also attends to medical features known to physicians. This is complemented by the machine's capability to spot subtle details that elude the human eye. In the future, such solutions will help doctors diagnose diseases and select treatment strategies.

mix_items.title: National study finds decline in drug use–associated heart infections but growing share involves stimulants
mix_items.summary: A new national study found that hospitalizations for serious heart infections associated with drug use are declining after years of increases, driven largely by a decrease in opioid-associated cases.

mix_items.title: 3D-printed implant prototype combines brain activity recording with targeted cooling
mix_items.summary: Researchers affiliated with the Leibniz Institute of Polymer Research Dresden (IPF) and the Else Kröner Fresenius Center (EKFZ) for Digital Health at TU Dresden have developed a 3D-printed implant prototype that combines the recording of brain activity with targeted cooling. The technology could pave the way for alternative approaches to treating drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The research is published in the journal Advanced Science.

mix_items.title: Guideline on shorter-course radiation therapy for localized prostate cancer updated
mix_items.summary: An updated clinical guideline from the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of hypofractionated radiation therapy for patients with localized prostate cancer. The guideline replaces ASTRO's 2018 recommendations and reflects a matured evidence base showing that shorter-course radiation therapy can maintain cancer control while reducing overall treatment burden for patients receiving definitive external beam radiation therapy (EBRT). The guideline was published in Practical Radiation Oncology.

mix_items.title: How our blood vessels age from within
mix_items.summary: With every heartbeat, blood is pumped through a vast network of vessels throughout our body, delivering vital oxygen, nutrients and other essential substances to even its most remote corners. But these vessels are far more than passive tubes: Their inner walls are covered by a thin layer of specialized cells called endothelial cells, which regulate blood flow, control what passes into surrounding tissues and help coordinate responses to injury.

mix_items.title: More than half of children under 5 exposed to hep B exposed via household contact
mix_items.summary: More than half of children younger than 5 years exposed to hepatitis B virus (HBV) are exposed by someone in their household other than their birth mother, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

mix_items.title: Rising rates of colorectal cancer found in nearly all age groups
mix_items.summary: Colorectal cancer rates are rising across younger and older age groups, according to a study published in NEJM Evidence.

mix_items.title: A doctor's take on new menopause guidelines
mix_items.summary: Many women I see in my practice have questions about menopause and hormone therapy. The newest guidelines from the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists (ACOG) bring some welcome clarity.

mix_items.title: IDSA: Cabotegravir + rilpivirine long-acting antiretroviral therapy beneficial in HIV
mix_items.summary: Cabotegravir + rilpivirine (CAB+RPV) long-acting (LA) antiretroviral therapy (ART) consistently maintains virologic suppression among virologically suppressed adults with HIV, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

mix_items.title: Deep brain stimulation improves new neuron maturation for memory
mix_items.summary: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has traditionally been used to treat movement disorders and more recently some mental health disorders such as certain forms of depression, but research has suggested it can affect learning and memory as well.

mix_items.title: Initial treatment for lower back pain is associated with subsequent risk of opioid use disorder and overdose
mix_items.summary: Adults on Medicaid who began treatment for a new bout of low back pain with a higher-dose opioid prescription were about two and a half times as likely to later show signs of opioid use disorder or overdose, according to a study conducted at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

mix_items.title: IDSA: Earlier introduction of HPV vaccine improves initiation, completion by age 13
mix_items.summary: Introducing the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine at ages 9 to 10 years rather than 11 to 12 years leads to a meaningful difference in initiation and completion of the vaccine series, including initiation and completion by age 13 years, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

mix_items.title: How blocking immune cell signals could make brain tumors easier to remove
mix_items.summary: In a new study published in Cancer Cell, researchers at VIB-KU Leuven reduced the spread of glioblastoma by interrupting specific interactions between the brain's immune cells and tumor cells. The discovery points to a possible new therapeutic strategy, in which blocking communication between immune and cancer cells makes tumors more contained and easier to remove.

mix_items.title: Do more cannabis stores near schools mean more teens use cannabis? Our research suggests the answer is complicated
mix_items.summary: When Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, one concern was that more legal stores would make cannabis easier for young people to access and encourage adolescent use. But does having more cannabis retailers near high schools actually mean more students use cannabis?

mix_items.title: Pathology research identifies potential new target for preventing brain metastasis
mix_items.summary: Research led by professor of pathology Mikhail Nikiforov, Ph.D., has identified a key mechanism that helps cancer cells spread to the brain, which may lead to a new target for future therapies. The findings were published in the journal Cell Reports in the article "SERINC2-mediated phosphatidylserine remodeling activates protrusion-localized AXL signaling to promote brain metastasis."

mix_items.title: Medicare's prior-authorization pilot test led to an immediate drop in use of services
mix_items.summary: For many years, traditional Medicare has operated almost entirely without prior authorization, a requirement that clinicians obtain approval before certain services will be covered. The practice is controversial because it adds paperwork, outside review and other barriers that can delay or deny coverage for recommended treatment. While prior authorization is widely used by commercial insurers and Medicare Advantage, traditional Medicare has historically almost never required it.

mix_items.title: Viruses obey the laws of physics—understanding why they infect people differently could lead to better treatments
mix_items.summary: The beauty of physics at the cellular scale is part of what draws biomedical engineers and biologists like us to the field of mechanobiology: the study of how physical forces influence biology.

mix_items.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
mix_items.summary: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.

mix_items.title: Blood pressure pregnancy clue could open door to new treatments
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust have uncovered a hidden defect in the tiny blood vessels of women with preeclampsia, a dangerous and common pregnancy complication that can threaten the lives of both mother and baby.

mix_items.title: Persian leopards hang on in the Caucasus despite landmines
mix_items.summary: There have been few sightings of the endangered Persian leopard in the Caucasus region over the past 20 years: just three in Georgia and 10 in Armenia. But scientists and conservationists are alert to one Persian leopard in particular, whom they’ve named Aren and who is presumed to have journeyed 240 kilometers (150 miles) through […]

mix_items.title: Higher medical fees increase expected pain and reduce willingness to book appointments
mix_items.summary: Rising out-of-pocket medical costs do more than drain a patient's bank account. New research from Carnegie Mellon University shows that high health care prices cause people to expect greater physical pain during medical procedures, driving many patients to skip necessary appointments altogether.

mix_items.title: Most childhood physical abuse perpetrated within the home, new study finds
mix_items.summary: New Curtin University–led research has revealed most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families—and before children turn 10.

mix_items.title: 40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
mix_items.summary: Forty years after the Chornobyl disaster, tiny radioactive particles still linger in the soil, carrying a dangerous legacy. Using powerful X-rays, scientists discovered that some of these particles have remained surprisingly stable, trapping radioactive substances inside instead of releasing them into the environment.

mix_items.title: Nearly 3,000 exploding stars challenge our understanding of the Universe
mix_items.summary: A massive analysis of 2,884 exploding stars has uncovered new evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the universe’s expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a cornerstone of modern cosmology and could reshape our understanding of how the universe works.

mix_items.title: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease.

mix_items.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.

mix_items.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
mix_items.summary: Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. The breakthrough could provide new insights into cancer, infectious diseases, and how drugs interact with cells.

mix_items.title: What went right this week: Indonesia’s plummeting poverty rate, plus more
mix_items.summary: Indonesia’s plummeting poverty rate, America’s largest wildlife bridge, and ‘a new era’ for the River Thames, plus more The post What went right this week: Indonesia’s plummeting poverty rate, plus more appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
mix_items.summary: Australia's normally dry, rust-colored outback has erupted into a spectacular carpet of wildflowers after unusually heavy rains, potentially producing its most impressive bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellite images capture the stunning transformation, which has even brought rare flowers to the grounds of a remote deep-space observatory.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.

mix_items.title: NASA spots a giant patch of Moon-like rock on Earth
mix_items.summary: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed a remarkable formation in Madagascar that looks surprisingly similar to the Moon’s bright highlands. Made of anorthosite, a rock abundant on the lunar surface, the formation dates back at least 600 million years and bears the scars of ancient continental collisions.

mix_items.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
mix_items.summary: Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.

mix_items.title: Earth’s center is moving, and NASA just measured it
mix_items.summary: Earth’s center of mass is constantly on the move, shifting by a few millimeters as enormous amounts of water, ice, and even air migrate around the planet with the seasons. NASA scientists have developed a more precise way to track these tiny swings using laser-ranging satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.
